definition: Machine translation is a sub-field of computational linguistics that investigates the use of software to translate text or speech from one natural language to another.
details: In the 1950s, machine translation became a reality in research, although references to the subject can be found as early as the 17th century. The Georgetown experiment, which involved successful fully automatic translation of more than sixty Russian sentences into English in 1954, was one of the earliest recorded projects. Researchers of the Georgetown experiment asserted their belief that machine translation would be a solved problem within a few years. In the Soviet Union, similar experiments were performed shortly after. Consequently, the success of the experiment ushered in an era of significant funding for machine translation research in the United States. The achieved progress was much slower than expected; in 1966, the ALPAC report found that ten years of research had not fulfilled the expectations of the Georgetown experiment and resulted in dramatically reduced funding. Interest grew in statistical models for machine translation, which became more common and also less expensive in the 1980s as available computational power increased. Although there exists no autonomous system of "fully automatic high quality translation of unrestricted text," there are many programs now available that are capable of providing useful output within strict constraints. Several of these programs are available online, such as Google Translate and the SYSTRAN system that powers AltaVista's BabelFish (which was replaced by Microsoft Bing translator in May 2012).

explainer.lead: The history of machine translation traces attempts to make software turn one natural language into another. Its early demonstrations raised hopes of a quick solution, but slower progress, funding cuts, and later statistical methods showed why useful translation is easier within limits than for unrestricted text.

tiers.eli5: Machine translation is like teaching a computer to retell a message in another language. A successful demonstration in 1954 made researchers think the problem would soon be solved, but translating language turned out to be much harder. Later computers and statistical methods improved the results, although unrestricted, high-quality automatic translation remained an unsolved goal.
tiers.practitioner: Machine translation is applied through online services such as Google Translate and historically through SYSTRAN, which powered AltaVista's BabelFish before Microsoft Bing translator replaced it in May 2012. It can provide useful output under strict constraints, but practitioners should not assume that a successful demonstration guarantees high-quality translation of unrestricted text. The field's history is a warning against estimating deployment readiness from early demos alone.
tiers.paperLevel: Machine translation studies software mappings from text or speech in a source natural language L_s to a target natural language L_t. The 1954 Georgetown experiment demonstrated fully automatic translation of more than sixty Russian sentences into English, but the 1966 ALPAC report found that a decade of research had not met the resulting expectations. Statistical models gained interest and became more common and less expensive in the 1980s as computational power increased, yet no autonomous system achieved fully automatic high-quality translation of unrestricted text.

explainer.example: In the 1954 Georgetown experiment, software successfully translated more than sixty Russian sentences into English without human intervention. Researchers took this result as evidence that machine translation might be solved within a few years, but the 1966 ALPAC report concluded that the intervening decade had not fulfilled those expectations.

explainer.intuition: The central lesson is that translating some sentences automatically is not the same as solving translation generally. Progress came in cycles: an impressive demonstration encouraged major funding, disappointing results reduced it, and greater computational power later made statistical approaches more practical.
howItWorks: References to machine translation appeared as early as the 17th century, before working research systems existed.
In 1954, the Georgetown experiment demonstrated fully automatic Russian-to-English translation and encouraged predictions of rapid success.
Similar Soviet experiments followed, while the demonstration helped bring significant research funding to the United States.
In 1966, the ALPAC report found that ten years of research had not fulfilled those expectations, leading to dramatically reduced funding.
In the 1980s, increased computational power helped statistical models become more common and less expensive.
explainer.whyItMatters: This history explains why machine translation developed through alternating optimism and disappointment rather than steady progress toward a quick solution. It also distinguishes useful systems operating under constraints from the still-unmet goal described as fully automatic high-quality translation of unrestricted text.
misconceptions: Machine translation did not begin with modern online services; research became a reality in the 1950s, with earlier references dating to the 17th century.
The Georgetown experiment did not solve general translation; it demonstrated success on more than sixty Russian sentences.
Reduced funding after the ALPAC report did not end the field, and statistical approaches later gained momentum.
